title: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: THIRD-PARTY SECURITY AUDITS OF NUCLEAR POWER PLANTS
body_text:
Adequate measures are in place to ensure the security of nuclear power plants. Periodic security assessments are conducted both internally and by AERB, at all Nuclear Power Plant sites including Kudankulam. Additionally, assessments of nuclear power plants are also conducted by external Government agencies. The observations made are reviewed; monitored and necessary upgrades are carried out for compliance.
In all nuclear power plants, state of the art security measures are in place. Besides other provisions, Electronic Security and Surveillance systems like Perimeter Intrusion Detection System, Access Control System, X-Ray Baggage Inspection System, CCTV Monitoring System, etc are in place at all operating Nuclear Power Plants. These systems are implemented as an integral part of the Nuclear Power Plants. The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) also conducts regulatory inspection in respect of nuclear security of all Nuclear Power Plants.
Cybersecurity of nuclear installations is accorded the highest priority. Continuous monitoring and surveillance mechanisms are in place to detect and respond to cyber threats. Appropriate preventive and protective measures including access controls, regular security audits, vulnerability assessments, incident response mechanisms and capacity-building programmes are implemented. Further, CERT-in enhances the national cyber security posture by issuing alerts and advisory on emerging cyber threats and vulnerabilities, coordinating incident response and advisory remedial measures to affected organisations and operating the National Cyber Coordination Centre (NCCC).
Emergency Preparedness Plans (EPPs) approved by the regulatory authority are put in place at all Nuclear Power Plant sites including Kudankulam. Periodic exercises are also carried out involving various stakeholders including, local administration, security agencies and nuclear plant authorities. Feedback from the exercises is used to validate and improve the emergency preparedness plans. Presently, off-site emergency preparedness exercises viz. Table Top, Integrated Command, Control & Response (ICCR) & Mock Exercises are carried out once in two years, once in three years and as per NDMA schedule, respectively. The NPP authorities are regularly conducting the exercises at stipulated frequency. The ICCR exercise at Kudankulam NPP site was conducted on 15 th April 2025. All the other NPP sites have also conducted their latest ICCR exercises since September, 2024 till date. For Kalpakkam site, the offsite emergency exercise has been conducted in ICCR (Integrated Command, Control & Response) mode on 17 th July 2026 with the initiating event from PFBR and this exercise involves Participation of District Administration.
This information was given by Union Minister of State for Prime Minister’s office and Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh, in a written reply in the Lok Sabha today.

NKR/AK/NM

enrichment.summary: In a written Lok Sabha reply, Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh stated that Indian nuclear power plants, including Kudankulam, have robust security measures including periodic AERB and external agency audits, electronic surveillance systems, and cybersecurity protocols coordinated with CERT-In. Emergency Preparedness Plans are regularly tested through Table Top, ICCR, and Mock exercises, with recent ICCR exercises conducted at Kudankulam (April 2025) and Kalpakkam (July 2026, involving the PFBR).
enrichment.context: Nuclear security and emergency preparedness are critical components of India's civil nuclear programme, governed primarily by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB), which was established under the Atomic Energy Act, 1962. India operates nuclear power plants under IAEA safeguards for certain reactors and follows a multi-layered security approach combining physical security (electronic surveillance, perimeter systems), cybersecurity, and disaster management protocols involving NDMA guidelines. The Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant, a joint India-Russia venture, has historically been a focus of security scrutiny given its scale and past cyberattack incidents (notably the 2019 malware incident affecting an administrative network, though not safety-critical systems). The mention of Kalpakkam's Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) is significant as it is part of India's indigenous fast breeder reactor programme under the second stage of the three-stage nuclear power programme, crucial for thorium utilization. Regular Integrated Command, Control & Response (ICCR) exercises reflect India's institutionalized approach to nuclear emergency management, coordinating Department of Atomic Energy facilities with district administrations and NDMA, drawing lessons from global precedents like Fukushima to strengthen offsite emergency response capabilities.

prelims_questions.question: Which of the following statements about India's nuclear security framework is correct, based on recent government disclosures?
options: The AERB has no role in conducting regulatory inspections of nuclear security at power plants
CERT-In operates the National Cyber Coordination Centre (NCCC) to enhance national cyber security posture
Emergency Preparedness Plans are only implemented at the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant
Mock exercises for nuclear emergency preparedness are conducted annually at all sites
prelims_questions.explanation: The release explicitly states that CERT-In operates the National Cyber Coordination Centre (NCCC) as part of enhancing national cybersecurity posture, including for nuclear installations.

prelims_questions.question: The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR), mentioned in context of the Kalpakkam emergency exercise, is associated with which stage of India's three-stage nuclear power programme?
options: First stage - Pressurized Heavy Water Reactors
Second stage - Fast Breeder Reactors using plutonium
PFBR is not part of the three-stage programme
prelims_questions.explanation: The PFBR at Kalpakkam is central to the second stage of India's three-stage nuclear power programme, which uses fast breeder reactors to utilize plutonium and produce more fissile material for eventual thorium utilization in the third stage.
